label: Blue Note
rationale: Contours is Sam Rivers's second Blue Note album as a leader: four of his own compositions, nine to twelve minutes each, recorded at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio on 21 May 1965 and held back until January 1967 [S1,S3,S4,S6] (obs). It is the record where Rivers — soprano and tenor saxophones and flute — took the post-bop frame of his debut Fuchsia Swing Song (already in the canon) and loosened the harmony and rhythm while keeping the swing: AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine calls it 'one of the high watermarks of the mid-'60s avant-garde movement' [S1,S2] (obs). Consensus as far as it goes, recorded honestly: AllMusic five stars, DownBeat four and a half, the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide four, the Encyclopedia of Popular Music four, the Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings three [S1] (obs). Session gravity is the strongest signal: Rivers with Freddie Hubbard, Herbie Hancock and Ron Carter — Hancock and Carter then in Miles Davis's quintet, with whom Rivers had just toured Japan in July 1964 — and Joe Chambers on drums, Tony Williams having been unable to make the date [S5,S6] (obs). Lineage: Chambers is the drummer on Andrew Hill's Judgment! and Bobby Hutcherson's Components, both already in this canon, and Rivers's brief Miles tenure is the bridge that put him on the bandstand the canon's mid-1960s records are built from (canon cross-reference, no source needed for the personnel overlap) [S6] (inf); Rivers wrote everything here, and the extended-form writing on this date is what he carried into the loft era [S6] (obs, as the article's account of his development). It still plays: the Tone Poet reissue sheet calls Van Gelder's recording ageless and describes the quintet's freedom as 'keeping a foot firmly planted in Post-Bop' [S5] (obs). Boundary note for the ballot: this is the borderline modal/avant territory the rubric flags as scope_call — Rivers fully embraced the avant-garde here, though Erlewine's review stresses that he did it in a way that would not upset hard bop loyalists [S1,S2] (obs). John rules.

personnel.name: Sam Rivers
personnel.notes: Leader and composer of all four titles. Doubles on soprano saxophone and flute: S6 hears soprano saxophone on 'Point Of Many Returns' (unison horn motif with Hubbard), tenor on the waltz-time 'Dance Of The Tripedal', flute on 'Euterpe' (with Hubbard muted), and tenor again on 'Mellifluous Cacophony'. Tenor saxophone is recorded as the instrument per the contract's doubling rule; S1/S3/S5 list the album's instrumentation as 'tenor, soprano sax, flute' without splitting it track by track.

personnel.name: Freddie Hubbard
personnel.notes: Open trumpet on 'Point Of Many Returns' and 'Dance Of The Tripedal', muted on 'Euterpe' (S6). The Tone Poet credit sheet (S5) prints the surname as 'Hubard'; this is a typographical error on that sheet, not a name variant in use.

personnel.name: Herbie Hancock
personnel.notes: Solos on all four titles (S6). Then a member of Miles Davis's quintet, as was Ron Carter (S6).

personnel.name: Ron Carter
personnel.notes: Walking bass and an unaccompanied passage on 'Point Of Many Returns'; solos on 'Mellifluous Cacophony' (S6).

personnel.name: Joe Chambers
personnel.notes: Deputising for Tony Williams, who could not make the date (S6). Solos on 'Mellifluous Cacophony' (S6).

personnel_record.notes: Single session: May 21, 1965, Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey — Englewood Cliffs, not Hackensack, the move having been July 1959 (S3). Four titles were cut (S3 master numbers 1582, 1583, 1584, 1585); the original LP carried all four, and the 2004 CD added an alternate take of 'Mellifluous Cacophony' (S1, S9) which is recorded here as track 5 with bonus_track and alternate_take set. The LP sides follow S5: side A 'Point Of Many Returns' / 'Dance Of The Tripedal', side B 'Euterpe' / 'Mellifluous Cacophony'. Timing sources differ slightly — S1 gives 9:20/10:07/11:43/8:58 and 9:04 for the alternate, S2 gives 49:23 for the expanded programme and the 2004 remaster runs about a second per track longer — the S1 figures are used. Track work is dated to the single session date; S3 lists the personnel with no per-title exclusions, and S5 lists the full quintet for the LP, so every musician is recorded as all-tracks with track_assignments_complete true. Production: producer Alfred Lion (S1, S5, S6) and engineer Rudy Van Gelder (S5 'Original engineer', with S6 describing the recording as made at Van Gelder's studio and S4 crediting him for the lacquer cut). Rivers's doubling on soprano saxophone and flute is carried in the personnel notes rather than as separate instrument rows, per the contract's doubling rule. Release year 1965 is the recording year, matching the canon's existing convention (e.g. Lee Morgan, The Sidewinder, recorded 1963 / released 1964, catalogued 1963); the LP itself appeared in January 1967 (S1, S4, S6).

scope_check.boundary_note: The post-bop/avant-garde boundary is in play: the album retains swing and post-bop grounding while extending toward the avant-garde.

ballot.case_for: The session brings Rivers together with Freddie Hubbard, Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter, and Joe Chambers, a consequential mid-1960s Blue Note network with direct ties to Miles Davis's band and other canon sessions (S3, S6). The four Rivers compositions extend the post-bop vocabulary toward freer forms while retaining swing; AllMusic calls the album a high watermark of the mid-'60s avant-garde, and the Tone Poet notes its post-bop grounding (S1, S2, S5).
ballot.case_against: The critical evidence is favorable but not uniformly canonical: AllMusic gives five stars and DownBeat 4.5, while the Penguin Guide gives three (S1), and the dossier supplies no direct evidence of broad placement on major canon lists. Its border position also cuts both ways: the freer writing may feel less settled to post-bop listeners, while its studio-bound restraint may seem less decisive than Rivers's later avant-garde work.
ballot.recommendation: John should decide whether this post-bop/avant-garde bridge belongs within the canon's permeable boundary, with the album's exceptional session gravity weighing strongly in its favor.
